inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Uniform triangular packings are not optimal for square containers due to boundary mismatch; they leave gaps that a centered non-uniform configuration can utilize.","Triangular lattices maintain equal minimum areas globally, whereas the square configuration relies on boundary effects to increase internal point distances.","The circular packing metric relies on radial distance, while minimum triangle area depends on planar affine properties (determinants), which are not strictly maximized by radial packing."],"overturn_conditions":["If the grid can be perturbed to break all collinearities while maintaining area > 0.005, the zero-area failure is overturned.","If a different grid resolution (e.g., 5x5) allows 13 points with no three collinear and min area > 0.005, the approach is validated.","If a non-grid symmetric arrangement (e.g., concentric squares) achieves a higher minimum area than the optimal triangular packing density analogue."],"shared_structure":["Both problems involve placing a fixed number of points in a bounded 2D container to maximize the minimum value of a distance/area metric.","Both seek to avoid configurations where points are too close or aligned, which minimizes the objective to zero.","Both use symmetric lattice-like arrangements as initial heuristic solutions."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_004"],"transfer_claims":["As with circle packing, the optimal point configuration for minimum triangle area will be highly symmetric and approach a regular lattice internally, but require boundary-specific adjustments.","The optimal minimum area will be bounded above by a density constant analogous to the packing density, suggesting 0.005 is a loose lower bound for n=13.","Random perturbations of a lattice will generally perform worse than optimized symmetric configurations, just as random circle packings are less dense than regular ones."]},"claim":"POINT 0.000000 0.000000

This results in a minimum triangle area of exactly zero.
